note: Case Workbench parameters and sources. Same discipline as the physiology engine (Milestone 8) and the theatre (Milestone 17): every number carries a status — cited (traceable to a source consulted during this build session, listed below), computed (arithmetic on cited values, derivation shown), calibrated (chosen inside a cited range, disclosed), or verify / project-convention (an authoring or workbench constant, visibly flagged, never presented as clinical fact). Sources C1-C9 and C12 are clinical literature consulted in-session; C10/C11 are ontology lookups performed in-session against the EBI Ontology Lookup Service; C13 collects the project's own module outputs this module links to. SNOMED CT appears nowhere in this module (design/07: excluded from the public repository entirely). LOINC codes likewise do not appear: design/07 fences LOINC into a separately-licensed data pack that is not in this repository, so labs carry local codes only. Milestone 22 addendum: sources C14-C16 and one further LR derivation (MRCP for retained common bile duct stone) were added for case 2 (case.post-op-jaundice.002), and the C10/C11 registers carry dated Milestone 22 addenda from the same in-session OLS queries. The workbench constants are unchanged.

parameters.note: A hypothesis is 'ruled out' on the workbench board when its evidence-updated posterior falls below this probability at a stage end. A workbench display convention, not a clinical quantity; no consulted source defines it and it is never presented as one.

An anchoring event is recorded when a learner board assigns at least this probability to a hypothesis the workbench has already ruled out (posterior below rule_out_threshold) at the same or an earlier stage. Design/07 names anchoring's cognitive family (the diagnostic-error literature it cites attributes ~70-75% of errors partly to cognitive factors) but defines no numeric threshold; this one is a project convention, flagged as such.

An ordered test is 'discriminating' if its results (a) move the leading hypothesis's workbench posterior by at least this amount, or (b) move any hypothesis across the rule-out threshold, or (c) change the top-ranked hypothesis. A test that settles a guideline criterion block (met or unmet) without meeting (a)-(c) is 'criteria-completing'. A test whose role is excluding a must-not-miss hypothesis without a quantified LR is 'safety-net'. Anything else is 'non-contributory'. These are bookkeeping rules for the debrief, defined here so the checker can recompute them; they are not clinical claims.

Workbench posteriors are computed by multiplying cited likelihood ratios onto declared priors, one hypothesis at a time (each published LR is a for/against statement about its own target condition versus the alternatives in its source studies), then normalising. This assumes conditional independence of findings, which is false in general — Murphy's sign and RUQ tenderness are not independent — and the board is therefore a teaching instrument, not a probability estimate for a real patient. C3's own conclusion stands over the whole mechanism: no single finding rules cholecystitis in or out, and the computed board never overrides the guideline criteria blocks, which are evaluated separately and reported alongside.

sources.citation: Yokoe M, Hata J, Takada T, et al. Tokyo Guidelines 2018: diagnostic criteria and severity grading of acute cholecystitis (with videos). J Hepatobiliary Pancreat Sci. 2018;25(1):41-54. PMID 29032636. DOI 10.1002/jhbp.515
sources.consulted: Criteria and severity tables as published (A: local signs — Murphy's sign, RUQ mass/pain/tenderness; B: systemic signs — fever, elevated CRP, elevated WBC; C: imaging findings characteristic of acute cholecystitis; suspected = one item in A + one item in B; definite = A + B + C. Grade III = any listed organ dysfunction; Grade II = WBC > 18,000/mm3, palpable tender RUQ mass, duration > 72 h, or marked local inflammation; Grade I = neither. TG18 flowchart: early laparoscopic cholecystectomy for Grade I where comorbidity/ASA conditions are met.)

sources.citation: Kiriyama S, Kozaka K, Takada T, et al. Tokyo Guidelines 2018: diagnostic criteria and severity grading of acute cholangitis (with videos). J Hepatobiliary Pancreat Sci. 2018;25(1):17-30. PMID 29032610
sources.consulted: Criteria table (A: systemic inflammation — fever and/or shaking chills, laboratory evidence of inflammatory response: abnormal WBC count, increased serum CRP; B: cholestasis — jaundice with total bilirubin >= 2 mg/dL, abnormal liver function tests: ALP, GGT, AST, ALT elevated; C: imaging — biliary dilatation, evidence of the etiology such as stricture, stone, stent. Suspected = one item in A + one item in either B or C; definite = A + B + C. The TG13 table quantifies A-2 as WBC < 4,000 or > 10,000/microL and CRP >= 1 mg/dL, and B-2 as enzymes > 1.5x the upper limit of normal.) Charcot's triad in the derivation cohort: sensitivity 26.4%, specificity 95.6% — specific but insensitive, which is why the criteria exist.

sources.consulted: Abstract and article text: no single clinical or laboratory finding rules acute cholecystitis in or out. The overall clinical impression's positive LR of 25-30 is reported in the paper but is NOT used by the workbench (it is an impression, not a finding).

sources.consulted: Diagnosis requires two of three: (1) abdominal pain consistent with acute pancreatitis (acute onset of persistent, severe, epigastric pain often radiating to the back); (2) serum lipase (or amylase) activity at least three times the upper limit of normal; (3) characteristic findings on cross-sectional imaging (CECT, or less commonly MRI or transabdominal ultrasound).

sources.citation: Birindelli A, Sartelli M, Di Saverio S, et al. 2020 WSES guidelines for the detection and management of bile duct injury during cholecystectomy. World J Emerg Surg. 2021;16:30. DOI 10.1186/s13017-021-00369-w (PMC8190978)
sources.consulted: Consulted in full text in-session (PMC8190978), key questions 3, 4, 6, 7 and Table 2. Classification (Table 2): Strasberg A = cystic duct leak or leaks from small ducts in the liver bed; B = occlusion of an aberrant right hepatic duct; C = leak from an aberrant right hepatic duct; D = lateral injury to the CBD; E subdivided by the Bismuth level: CBD stump > 2 cm = Bismuth I / Strasberg E1; stump < 2 cm = II / E2; ceiling of the confluence intact = III / E3; ceiling destroyed = IV / E4; type I-III plus stricture of an isolated right duct = V / E5. Major BDIs (Strasberg E) are associated with tissue loss (e.g. the common bile duct is clipped and transected) and require Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy (KQ4 statement 4.2: hepaticojejunostomy is the treatment of choice for major BDIs). Presentation (KQ6 review): the two most frequent scenarios are bile leakage and bile duct obstruction; cholestatic jaundice with choluria, fecal acholia, and pruritus are the most common signs of the obstruction/stricture picture; in complete occlusion bilirubin rises; ALP and bilirubin are the early cholestasis markers. Investigations (statements 6.1-6.3): prompt investigation of alarm symptoms (fever, abdominal pain, distention, jaundice, nausea, vomiting); LFTs including bilirubin, AST, ALT, ALP, GGT; CT first-line for collections and ductal dilation, complemented by CE-MRCP for exact visualisation, localisation, and classification. MRCP is the 'gold standard' for complete morphological evaluation of the biliary tree, showing anatomy proximal and distal to the injury. ERCP limits: it does not visualise ducts upstream of an obstructing lesion, and endoscopic treatments for bile leaks are ineffective 'except in the case of transection of the common bile duct or common hepatic duct' (review text: endoscopic therapy cannot bridge a transection). Hepatobiliary scintigraphy is more sensitive and specific than US/CT for bile leaks but has poor spatial resolution and pitfalls in large duct defects. Postoperative management (statements 7.3-7.5): major BDI (E1-E2) diagnosed within 72 h — referral to an HPB-expert centre if expertise is unavailable locally, urgent Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy may follow; diagnosed between 72 h and 3 weeks — percutaneous drainage of fluid collections whenever present, targeted antibiotics, nutritional support, PTBD may be useful for septic patients with complete CBD obstruction, and Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy after a minimum of 3 weeks once the acute situation has resolved; late-presenting stricture — Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy. Antibiotics (KQ5 review): in biliary obstruction without bile leak or signs of sepsis, antibiotic therapy may not be required.

sources.citation: Comparative Diagnostic Accuracy of Clinical Assessment, Computed Tomography (CT), and Magnetic Resonance Imaging With Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography (MRI/MRCP) in Evaluating Common Bile Duct Stones. Cureus. 2025;17(10):e94572. PMID 41169603 (PMC12569963)
sources.consulted: Abstract and results consulted in-session. Single-centre retrospective study, 691 adults evaluated for suspected choledocholithiasis, stone prevalence 45%, reference standard = definitive surgical/procedural diagnoses. MRI/MRCP: sensitivity 92.7%, specificity 91.9%, accuracy 92.3% — the most accurate of the modalities compared (CT 73.2%/82.9%; clinical assessment 71.1%/87.1%). The workbench's MRCP likelihood ratios are computed from these two numbers (see lr_derivations). This is a single study, not a meta-analysis, and the derivation is labelled with that limitation wherever used.
